subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage: In the courtyard of a mud-walled house, two-year-old Neelam was banging a steel spoon on an upturned bowl. Her mother Swati, hands floury from the morning rotis, gently lifted the spoon away. Neelam's eyebrows dropped, her lower lip pushed out, and she glared at the spoon in Swati's fingers. Swati crouched down. “You're cross. You wanted the spoon.” Neelam sniffed, leaned her whole weight against Swati's knee, still pouting, and lifted both arms to be picked up.

qa.q: What did Swati take away from Neelam?
qa.a: A steel spoon that Neelam had been banging on an upturned bowl.

qa.q: What might Neelam have been feeling when she lifted her arms, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: Most likely she felt frustrated about losing the spoon and wanted comfort, since she leaned on Swati and asked to be held. Another reading is that she was simply tired and wanted to be carried. 🙂

qa.q: What small step could Swati take next?
qa.a: She could keep naming the feeling in simple words, hold Neelam for a moment, and then offer a different safe thing to bang, such as a wooden spoon.

qa.q: How might Swati see Neelam's pout?
qa.a: Swati is likely to see it as a young child's honest signal of being upset and wanting closeness, not as a plan to get her way.

grounding: The toddler's frown and pout after the spoon is taken shows frustration and a wish for comfort, and the mother names the feeling.

subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage: Tomas, twenty months old, was filling a red bucket with sand at the park when an older boy scooped it up to carry to the water tap. Tomas's brows drew together, his mouth turned down, and his lip stuck out as he stared after the bucket. Then he turned and looked at his father. Mateo knelt beside him. “That was your bucket, and you're frustrated.” Tomas kept scowling but toddled into Mateo's arms and stayed there until the boy brought the bucket back.

qa.q: Where was Tomas when his bucket was taken?
qa.a: At the park, where he was filling a red bucket with sand.

qa.q: What does Tomas's look toward his father suggest he wanted?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted comfort or help, and the scowl shows frustration. It could also have been plain surprise at the sudden loss, since he had no time to react before the boy walked off.

qa.q: What could Mateo try if the bucket had not come back?
qa.a: He could keep naming the feeling, stay close, and steer Tomas gently toward another digging toy so the upset has somewhere to go.

qa.q: What might the older boy have been thinking?
qa.a: He may have thought the bucket was free to use and not realised Tomas minded. Bringing it back suggests he noticed Tomas's face and father.

grounding: The toddler scowls and pouts when his bucket is taken, and the father names the frustration and offers comfort.

subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage: I'm Ankita, from the flat upstairs, and I was coming down the stairs when it happened. Little Rukmini had a red toy tractor, and her older cousin snatched it to run it along the railing. Her face crumpled into a deep scowl, her lower lip pushed right out and her fists went stiff. She didn't grab it back. Her Amma knelt and said, "You're cross. Your tractor went away." Rukmini leaned into her shoulder. I couldn't tell if she wanted the tractor more or the cuddle.

qa.q: Who took Rukmini's red toy tractor?
qa.a: Her older cousin snatched it to run it along the railing.

qa.q: What might Rukmini's scowl and pushed-out lip suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely frustration at losing the tractor, shown by the deep scowl and stiff fists; leaning into Amma suggests she also wanted comfort, so it may have been sadness as much as anger.

qa.q: Which part of Amma's response helped, and why?
qa.a: Kneeling down and naming the feeling ("You're cross") helped, because Rukmini calmed enough to lean in for comfort instead of fighting for the toy.

qa.q: How does Ankita, watching from the stairs, read the moment?
qa.a: Ankita sees the scowl clearly but is not sure whether Rukmini mostly wanted the tractor back or the cuddle.

grounding: A toddler's scowl and pout when a toy is taken, read as frustration and a wish for comfort, with the feeling named by a caregiver.

subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage:
Monday: when Ganga lifted her out of the bath, Alka scowled and kicked. "You're angry. You wanted more splashing," said Ganga, wrapping her in the towel.
Thursday: Ganga said no to a second banana before dinner. Alka pouted, dropped her chin and stared at the floor. Ganga sat beside her. "Sad and cross. I know."
Sunday: the park swing was taken. Alka frowned, looked up at Ganga and said, "Cross!" Then she held out her arms.

qa.q: What did Alka say at the park on Sunday?
qa.a: She looked up at Ganga and said, "Cross!" and then held out her arms.

qa.q: How can you tell Alka was feeling more able to handle her frustration by Sunday?
qa.a: By Sunday she named the feeling herself with the word "Cross!" instead of only scowling, and then reached out for comfort, which suggests she felt disappointed but more settled.

qa.q: What small habit of Ganga's helped Alka over the week?
qa.a: Ganga named the feeling each time, such as "angry" or "sad and cross", and stayed close, so Alka had words to use.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had called the pout "drama" and walked away?
qa.a: Alka would get no word for her frustration and no comfort, so she might keep scowling and kicking instead of asking for a hug.

grounding: Repeated moments where a toddler's frown or pout at a refused wish is named by a caregiver until the child uses the word herself.

subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage:
The balloon seller at the colony market in Pune had a bunch of shiny red ones. Avni pointed and tugged. "Not today," said Chandrika, her mother, and walked on. Avni stopped dead. Her brows pulled down, her mouth turned into a tight pout, and she sat on the pavement.
A passing man muttered, "She's playing you."
Chandrika crouched. "You wanted the red balloon. You feel sad." Avni's pout wobbled and she lifted her arms to be carried.

qa.q: Where did Avni see the red balloons?
qa.a: At the colony market in Pune, where the balloon seller had a bunch of shiny red ones.

qa.q: What was Avni most likely feeling when she sat on the pavement?
qa.a: Frustrated and disappointed about the balloon, shown by her pulled-down brows and tight pout; lifting her arms suggests she also wanted comfort rather than trying to trick her mother. 🥺

qa.q: What would you advise a parent in Chandrika's place?
qa.a: Stay calm, crouch to the child's level and name the feeling, as Chandrika did, while keeping the "no".

qa.q: Why might the passing man react differently from Chandrika?
qa.a: He only saw a child sitting down in protest and guessed manipulation, while Chandrika knew Avni and read the pout as sadness.

grounding: A toddler's frown and pout at a refused wish, read as frustration and a wish to be comforted rather than a trick.

subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage:
“Jatin, give it back. She was playing with that.”
“But it's my truck, Mummy!”
Elizabeth's lower lip pushed out. Her eyebrows pulled down hard and she scowled at the truck in her brother's hands. Then she lifted both arms towards Mummy.
“Oh, you look cross,” Mummy said, picking her up. “You're frustrated. Jatin took the truck.”
“She's just being dramatic,” said Jatin.
“No, she's telling us how she feels. Can she have a turn after you?”
Jatin sighed. “Two minutes.”

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do with her arms after scowling at the truck?
qa.a: She lifted both arms towards Mummy.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she pouted and scowled?
qa.a: She was most likely frustrated that the truck was taken; lifting her arms suggests she also wanted comfort, not that she was putting on a show.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Elizabeth with the big feeling?
qa.a: Mummy picked her up and named the feeling, "You're frustrated," which gives Elizabeth a word for it, then arranged a turn.

qa.q: How does Jatin see Elizabeth's pout at first?
qa.a: Jatin thinks she is being dramatic, until Mummy explains the pout is her way of showing how she feels.

grounding: It shows a toddler scowling and pouting when a toy is taken, signalling frustration and a wish for comfort, and a parent naming the feeling.
